11.1 — Poultry, broilers and layers
Theory
Understand the idea

Poultry are domesticated birds kept for products such as meat and eggs. Chickens are a major commercial poultry species, although other domesticated birds may also be raised in agricultural systems. Poultry production is organised according to the product being produced and the needs of the birds.

Broiler production focuses on chickens raised for meat. Layer production focuses on chickens kept for egg production. These are different production goals, so the birds, housing, feeding, monitoring and management systems may also differ. The words broiler and layer describe production purpose rather than the appearance of a bird in a single photograph.

Selective breeding is the planned selection of parent animals with measured traits that may support a production goal. In broiler systems, selection goals may relate to meat-production traits. In layer systems, selection goals may relate to egg-production traits. However, a breeding goal does not guarantee the same result in every bird.

Hybrids are produced through planned crosses between selected breeding lines. A hybrid may be developed to combine useful characteristics or improve measured production traits. Hybrid performance still depends on genetics, management, health and environmental conditions. The word hybrid should not be treated as proof that a bird will always outperform every purebred bird.

Pure breeds may be used in small-scale production, exhibition, breeding programs or dual-purpose contexts. A dual-purpose bird may be considered for both meat and eggs, but suitability still depends on the particular system and goal. Pure breeds also show variation between individual birds.

A strong comparison identifies the production goal, the evidence used to measure performance and the conditions under which the evidence was collected. Photographs may show visible features, but they cannot prove whether a bird is a broiler, layer, hybrid or pure breed, or confirm its production performance. Reliable conclusions require records and trustworthy supporting information.

Key takeaways

Poultry are domesticated birds kept for products such as meat and eggs.

Broilers are raised for meat, while layers are kept for egg production.

Selective breeding and hybrids aim to support measured production traits but do not guarantee performance.

Genetics, management and environment all influence poultry outcomes.

Knowledge check

What is poultry?
A. Domesticated birds kept for products such as meat and eggs
B. Only chickens raised for meat
C. Wild birds living near farms
D. Any animal kept in a shed

Answer: A. Domesticated birds kept for products such as meat and eggs
Correct feedback: Correct. Poultry are domesticated birds kept for agricultural products such as meat and eggs.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening sentence and identify the broad group being defined.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

What is the main production goal of broiler systems?
A. Meat production
B. Egg production
C. Wool production
D. Milk production

Answer: A. Meat production
Correct feedback: Correct. Broiler production focuses on chickens raised for meat.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Compare the definitions of broiler and layer production in the second paragraph.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

What is the main production goal of layer systems?
A. Egg production
B. Meat production only
C. Feather production
D. Breeding wild birds

Answer: A. Egg production
Correct feedback: Correct. Layer production focuses on chickens kept for eggs.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the sentence that distinguishes layers from broilers.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

Why may broiler and layer systems be managed differently?
A. They have different production goals
B. All chickens require identical systems
C. Appearance determines every management choice
D. One system produces both products in the same way

Answer: A. They have different production goals
Correct feedback: Correct. Different goals can lead to differences in housing, feeding, monitoring and management.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on how production purpose affects system organisation.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

What is selective breeding?
A. Planned selection of parents with measured traits
B. Choosing birds only by colour
C. Allowing only random mating
D. Identifying birds from photographs

Answer: A. Planned selection of parents with measured traits
Correct feedback: Correct. Selective breeding uses measured traits to choose parent animals for a production goal.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph defining planned parent selection.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

What is a poultry hybrid?
A. A bird produced from a planned cross between selected lines
B. A bird identified only by appearance
C. A wild bird kept near poultry
D. A pure breed with no selected parents

Answer: A. A bird produced from a planned cross between selected lines
Correct feedback: Correct. Hybrids result from planned crosses between selected breeding lines.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Look for the definition in the paragraph beginning “Hybrids are produced”.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

Why is hybrid performance not guaranteed?
A. Genetics, management, health and environment all influence outcomes
B. Every hybrid is genetically identical
C. Management has no effect on birds
D. Hybrid labels prove production results

Answer: A. Genetics, management, health and environment all influence outcomes
Correct feedback: Correct. Several interacting factors affect the performance of each bird.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the factors listed after the explanation of hybrid breeding.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

Where might pure breeds be used?
A. Small-scale, exhibition or dual-purpose contexts
B. Only large commercial broiler systems
C. Only egg-processing factories
D. Only wild-bird conservation

Answer: A. Small-scale, exhibition or dual-purpose contexts
Correct feedback: Correct. Pure breeds may be used in several small-scale, breeding, exhibition or dual-purpose settings.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph explaining possible uses of pure breeds.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

What does dual-purpose mean in this context?
A. A bird may be considered for both meat and eggs
B. A bird is guaranteed to excel in every trait
C. A bird is both wild and domesticated
D. A bird belongs to two farms

Answer: A. A bird may be considered for both meat and eggs
Correct feedback: Correct. Dual-purpose refers to possible use for both meat and egg production.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the two agricultural products named in the theory.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

Why can a photograph not prove poultry production performance?
A. Performance requires records and supporting evidence
B. Every bird looks identical
C. Photographs include breeding records
D. Appearance guarantees production purpose

Answer: A. Performance requires records and supporting evidence
Correct feedback: Correct. A photograph shows visible features but cannot confirm genetics or measured production results.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the final paragraph and separate visible observations from performance evidence.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

Written evidence

Prompt: Explain the difference between broiler and layer production and identify one way their management may differ.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Broiler production raises chickens for meat, while layer production keeps chickens for egg production. Because their production goals differ, their feeding, housing, monitoring or other management systems may also be organised differently.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

Prompt: Explain why a hybrid chicken cannot be assumed to outperform every purebred chicken.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: A hybrid is produced through a planned cross between selected lines and may be developed for useful measured traits. However, performance also depends on genetics, management, health and environmental conditions. Individual birds vary, so hybrid status does not guarantee that every hybrid will outperform every purebred bird.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

Source boundary

Teach  poultry categories, production goals, selective breeding, hybrids and pure breeds conceptually. Do not ask students to identify birds from photographs, provide current industry figures or guarantee hybrid, breed or production performance. Any practical poultry activity must be teacher authorised and supervised.

Sources

Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/

11.2 — A poultry supply chain and location decisions
Theory
Understand the idea

A poultry supply chain describes how products move from production to consumers. A generic chicken-meat or egg supply chain begins with breeding and hatching, supported by feed suppliers and other production inputs. Birds are then reared for meat production or managed for egg laying, depending on the production goal.

After rearing or laying, products move to collection and processing. Eggs are collected before packing, while chicken meat moves through processing before packaging. These stages prepare products for transport, retail businesses, food-service businesses and finally consumers. At each stage, outputs from one part of the chain become inputs for the next.

Several resources influence where poultry production and processing are located. Feed and reliable water supplies are essential because birds require ongoing nutrition and care. Energy supports many production and processing activities, while labour provides planning, monitoring and day-to-day management. Biosecurity is also important because reducing the risk of disease introduction and spread supports the whole supply chain.

Processing capacity and transport connections influence where products can move efficiently through the system. Market access is also important because products need practical pathways to retailers, food-service businesses and consumers. These factors work together rather than acting independently.

Chicken meat and eggs are perishable products, so coordination across the supply chain is important. Processing, packing, transport, storage and retail stages are organised so products move under suitable conditions. Cold-chain management helps maintain product quality during movement, but the exact conditions depend on the product and current requirements.

Location decisions should therefore be explained using evidence. Students can compare locations by considering feed, water, energy, labour, biosecurity, processing capacity, transport and market access. A strong explanation recognises that no single factor guarantees success and that different production systems may respond differently to local conditions.

Key takeaways

The poultry supply chain links breeding, production, processing, transport, retail and consumers.

Feed, water, energy, labour and biosecurity all influence production and location decisions.

Processing capacity, transport and market access affect how products move through the supply chain.

Perishability requires coordinated movement and suitable cold-chain management rather than assumptions about one factor.

Knowledge check

What is the first stage in the generic poultry supply chain described?
A. Breeding and hatching
B. Retail sale
C. Consumer use
D. Food service

Answer: A. Breeding and hatching
Correct feedback: Correct. The supply chain begins with breeding and hatching before birds are reared or managed for production.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph and identify the first stage in the chain.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

What happens after birds are reared or managed for laying?
A. Collection and processing
B. Retail purchase
C. Consumer preparation
D. Feed production begins

Answer: A. Collection and processing
Correct feedback: Correct. Products move to collection and processing before packing and transport.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Look at the sequence described in the second paragraph.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Why are feed and water important in poultry production?
A. Birds require ongoing nutrition and care
B. They replace transport
C. They remove the need for labour
D. They guarantee production success

Answer: A. Birds require ongoing nutrition and care
Correct feedback: Correct. Feed and water are essential resources that support poultry production.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Choose the reason connected directly with the needs of the birds.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

What role does labour have in the supply chain?
A. Planning, monitoring and day-to-day management
B. Replacing biosecurity
C. Eliminating transport
D. Guaranteeing product quality

Answer: A. Planning, monitoring and day-to-day management
Correct feedback: Correct. Labour supports planning, monitoring and everyday production activities.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph describing resources that influence location.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Why is biosecurity important?
A. It helps reduce the risk of disease introduction and spread
B. It replaces feed and water
C. It guarantees identical production outcomes
D. It removes the need for processing

Answer: A. It helps reduce the risk of disease introduction and spread
Correct feedback: Correct. Biosecurity supports the supply chain by reducing disease risks.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the purpose of biosecurity within production systems.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

How can processing capacity influence location?
A. It affects how products move through the supply chain
B. It determines the colour of packaging
C. It replaces transport
D. It guarantees market demand

Answer: A. It affects how products move through the supply chain
Correct feedback: Correct. Processing capacity helps determine how efficiently products move through the system.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph about processing, transport and market access.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Why is market access important?
A. Products need practical pathways to buyers
B. It guarantees higher prices
C. It replaces production planning
D. It determines the breed of poultry

Answer: A. Products need practical pathways to buyers
Correct feedback: Correct. Market access connects producers with retailers, food-service businesses and consumers.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Choose the option that relates to getting products to buyers.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Why do perishable products require coordinated movement?
A. Quality depends on organised handling through the supply chain
B. They never need transport
C. They can be stored indefinitely
D. They eliminate the need for packing

Answer: A. Quality depends on organised handling through the supply chain
Correct feedback: Correct. Perishable products require coordinated handling as they move through the supply chain.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph explaining perishability and coordination.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

What does cold-chain management help maintain?
A. Suitable product conditions during movement
B. The location of breeding farms
C. The price of products
D. The number of consumers

Answer: A. Suitable product conditions during movement
Correct feedback: Correct. Cold-chain management helps maintain suitable product conditions while products move through the chain.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the purpose of cold-chain management rather than market outcomes.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Which statement best matches the theory?
A. Location decisions should consider several interacting factors
B. Feed alone determines every location
C. Transport alone guarantees success
D. One production system suits every location

Answer: A. Location decisions should consider several interacting factors
Correct feedback: Correct. Strong location decisions consider multiple interacting resources and constraints.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory explains that no single factor guarantees a successful location.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Written evidence

Prompt: Trace a generic chicken-meat or egg supply chain from breeding to consumers and identify three resources that support the system.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: The supply chain begins with breeding and hatching, followed by rearing or egg laying. Products then move through collection, processing, packing, transport, retail or food service and finally to consumers. Important supporting resources include feed, water, labour, energy, biosecurity and transport.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Prompt: Explain why two different locations might both be suitable for poultry production using at least four factors from the theory.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: One location may have reliable feed, water, labour and processing capacity, while another may have strong transport links, market access, energy supply and good biosecurity arrangements. Suitability depends on how these factors work together rather than on one factor alone, so different locations can support poultry production in different ways.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Chicken Meat Federation — Industry overview: https://chicken.org.au/our-industry/industry-overview/; Food  Standards Australia New Zealand — Primary production and processing standards: https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/primary-production-and-processing

Source boundary

Teach  the poultry supply chain and location decisions conceptually. Do not provide operational processing procedures, cold-chain settings, local production advice, company comparisons or current industry statistics. Any practical activities must be teacher authorised and supervised.

sections.content:

11.3 — Layer systems, welfare indicators and trade-offs
Theory
Understand the idea

Layer systems are organised in different ways to produce eggs. Broad examples include cage, barn and free-range systems. A fair comparison applies the same criteria to each system rather than assuming that one label proves better welfare.

Useful criteria include opportunities for movement and behaviour, protection from weather and predators, monitoring, disease and biosecurity exposure, land and infrastructure needs, egg collection and management. Cage systems generally use enclosed housing with controlled movement and organised egg collection. Barn systems keep birds indoors with more shared floor space and opportunities for movement within the building. Free-range systems provide access to outdoor areas as well as shelter. These are broad descriptions, and individual enterprises may differ.

Each system involves trade-offs. Greater outdoor access may provide more opportunities for movement and some natural behaviours, while also increasing exposure to weather, predators and environmental disease risks. More enclosed systems may support close monitoring, environmental control and organised egg collection, but may provide different movement and behaviour opportunities. Land, labour, infrastructure and management demands also vary.

Welfare is an outcome assessed through multiple indicators. Animal-based indicators can include behaviour, health observations, injury evidence and signs of comfort or distress. Resource and management indicators can include access to feed and water, housing condition, shelter, monitoring and records. The presence of one resource, or the name of the system, cannot prove the complete welfare outcome.

A defensible conclusion applies the same criteria to all systems, cites relevant evidence, explains trade-offs and acknowledges uncertainty. It avoids claiming that cage, barn or free-range production is universally best.

The Australian Poultry Standards and Guidelines have been nationally endorsed, but state and territory governments are responsible for implementation. Current requirements for a particular location must therefore be confirmed from the relevant authority. This section provides conceptual comparison only and does not give local procedures.

Key takeaways

Cage, barn and free-range systems should be compared using the same criteria.

Each layer system involves trade-offs among behaviour opportunities, protection, monitoring, biosecurity, land and management.

Welfare is assessed using multiple animal-based and resource or management indicators.

National poultry standards are implemented by states and territories, so current local requirements must be confirmed.

Knowledge check

What makes a comparison of layer systems fair?
A. Applying the same criteria to each system
B. Choosing the preferred label first
C. Comparing only egg colour
D. Assuming outdoor access proves welfare

Answer: A. Applying the same criteria to each system
Correct feedback: Correct. Fair comparisons apply consistent criteria to cage, barn and free-range systems.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph and identify how bias can be reduced.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Poultry Standards and Guidelines: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/standards-guidelines/poultry; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which is a useful criterion for comparing layer systems?
A. Movement and behaviour opportunities
B. Package advertising
C. Egg brand popularity
D. Farm logo design

Answer: A. Movement and behaviour opportunities
Correct feedback: Correct. Movement and behaviour opportunities are relevant to system comparison.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Choose a feature connected with housing, management or welfare evidence.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Poultry Standards and Guidelines: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/standards-guidelines/poultry; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which broad feature is associated with barn systems?
A. Birds are housed indoors with shared floor space
B. Birds remain outdoors at all times
C. Birds are identified by egg colour
D. No monitoring is required

Answer: A. Birds are housed indoors with shared floor space
Correct feedback: Correct. Barn systems generally house birds indoors with opportunities for movement within the building.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the broad descriptions of cage, barn and free-range systems.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Poultry Standards and Guidelines: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/standards-guidelines/poultry; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which broad feature is associated with free-range systems?
A. Access to outdoor areas as well as shelter
B. No exposure to weather
C. No need for biosecurity
D. Guaranteed welfare outcomes

Answer: A. Access to outdoor areas as well as shelter
Correct feedback: Correct. Free-range systems provide outdoor access along with shelter.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Outdoor access is a system feature, but it does not remove risks or guarantee outcomes.
Source: Authorised Module 11 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1nOUMPmjttHC8VkDE2btHmyFuLo-VTLqkJeFKDhKJatE/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Poultry Standards and Guidelines: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/standards-guidelines/poultry; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

What is a possible trade-off of greater outdoor access?
A. More behaviour opportunities but greater weather or predator exposure
B. Less movement and no environmental exposure
C. Guaranteed disease prevention
D. No land management requirements

Answer: A. More behaviour opportunities but greater weather or predator exposure
Correct feedback: Correct. Outdoor access may increase behaviour opportunities while also creating exposure risks.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the trade-off paragraph and identify both a benefit and a limitation.

Written evidence

Prompt: Compare two layer systems using four common criteria and explain one trade-off without ranking either system as universally best.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: A barn and free-range system can be compared using movement opportunities, protection from weather, monitoring and land needs. Free-range birds have outdoor access, while barn birds remain within sheltered housing. A trade-off is that outdoor access may increase behaviour opportunities but also increase weather and predator exposure. The stronger choice depends on animal observations, management evidence and the production context.

Prompt: Explain why welfare cannot be judged from the words cage, barn or free-range alone.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: A system label describes broad housing arrangements but does not show how birds respond over time. Welfare assessment requires animal-based indicators such as behaviour, health and injury evidence, together with resource and management indicators such as feed, water, shelter, monitoring and records.

Source boundary

Teach  cage, barn and free-range layer systems through consistent comparison criteria, trade-offs and multiple welfare indicators. Do not provide stocking densities, prices, local procedures, legal instructions or universal welfare rankings. Current state or territory requirements must be confirmed separately.
